strengths: Clearly identifies and addresses a real problem: the temporal resolution mismatch between speech and text tokens in joint speech-text modeling
Achieves state-of-the-art results on Spoken QA benchmarks (S→T: 75.1 vs 74.7 for Kimi-Audio; S→S: 55.5 vs 54.9 for VITA-Audio)
Demonstrates significant computational efficiency gains (approximately 50% reduction in GPU hours with grouping factor k=5)
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation including extensive ablations, data scaling studies, and computational resource analysis that clearly demonstrate each component's contribution
Well-designed architecture combining grouping for input efficiency with Speech Refined Head for output quality
Practical contributions including multiple modality interaction patterns and system prompts for flexible control
Strong promise of reproducibility with planned code and checkpoint release
Generally well-written with clear structure, good figures, and detailed implementation details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (grouping, ungrouping, CoM-Mixing) are largely incremental combinations of existing techniques rather than fundamental innovations
Narrow evaluation scope limited to Spoken Question Answering benchmarks; no human evaluation or assessment of general conversational quality and naturalness
Marginal improvements over prior SOTA (0.4 points on S→T, 0.6 on S→S average) raise questions about statistical significance and practical impact
Speech quality remains a significant limitation (UTMOS 3.86 vs 4.33 for GLM-4-Voice) due to reliance on HuBERT semantic tokens, with no proposed solution within the current framework
Latency analysis insufficient: claims about 'low-latency, real-time applications' lack concrete inference latency measurements and comparisons with baselines

Incomplete technical justification: why ungrouping+SRH is superior to alternatives not clearly explained; grouping factor k=5 selection methodology unclear; time-splitting operation inadequately explained

Data composition concerns: significant portion of training data is synthetically generated; exact composition unclear; different baselines may use different data amounts/types, complicating fair comparison
CoM-Mixing contribution primarily data augmentation rather than methodological innovation; similar gains might be achievable through other augmentation strategies
Missing analysis: no error analysis, failure modes, investigation of which modality pairs are most challenging, or concrete examples of prosody/emotion control despite claims
Inconsistent experimental design: different learning rates for different models without clear justification; some baseline results from other papers with potentially different experimental setups

strengths: Strong empirical results achieving SOTA on two major benchmarks (OpenAudioBench: 69.24 vs. 69.08, Big Bench Audio: 66.3 vs. 55.2) with substantial margins over prior work

Well-motivated dual-resolution speech representation mechanism that effectively addresses the frame rate mismatch between speech (25Hz) and text (~3Hz) tokens, reducing computational costs by ~50% without performance degradation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four benchmarks with good ablation studies (Table 4) demonstrating the contribution of key components (CSE, SRH, SRH-Pretraining, CoM-Mixing)
Significant practical efficiency gains: 5Hz frame rate vs. 12.5-25Hz in competitors, with 45 hours training on 64 A800 GPUs, enabling broader accessibility
Strong speech quality preservation: UTMOS score of 4.29 remains competitive despite low frame rate, demonstrating the effectiveness of the SRH design
Well-designed training strategies (CoM-Mixing for curriculum learning, Core-Cocktail for LLM knowledge retention) are well-motivated and empirically validated
Detailed implementation information and extensive appendices support reproducibility efforts
Clear presentation of the architecture and methodology with good motivation for design choices
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: individual components are largely adaptations from prior work (grouping from Chen et al. 2024a, CoM from Zhang et al. 2023a, model merging from Xiao et al. 2024); main contribution (DRSR) is somewhat incremental in combining these ideas

Significant speech-text alignment degradation: ASR-WER of 11.2 substantially worse than Qwen2.5-Omni (3.48), undermining claims of high-quality speech generation; paper acknowledges this but only suggests feeding text to SRH as future work, suggesting this should have been addressed in current work

Heavy reliance on synthetic training data: ~26K hours synthesized via CosyVoice, raising concerns about bias toward CosyVoice's style and unclear attribution of improvements to architecture vs. data quality; no fair-condition comparison with baselines using identical data

Evaluation methodology concerns: (1) Different models trained on different data/sizes complicating fair comparison, (2) GLM4-Voice results from citation rather than author reproduction, (3) Limited speech quality evaluation (only UTMOS and ASR-WER, no human evaluation), (4) No statistical significance testing or error bars reported

Insufficient analysis of core technical contributions: (1) No systematic comparison of ungrouping approaches, (2) Core-Cocktail with α=0 seems extreme—insufficient α ablation, (3) No comparison of dual-resolution vs. simply using 5Hz throughout without grouping/ungrouping, (4) Limited SRH architecture justification
Frame rate reporting lacks clarity: the FR(In/Out) comparison across models is somewhat confusing; unclear if 5Hz is fundamentally novel vs. an engineering choice

Missing reproducibility elements: Model unlikely to be released soon, training requires inaccessible computational resources (64 A800 GPUs), frozen dependence on CosyVoice components limit community reproduction

CoM-Mixing strategy insufficiently analyzed: improvements in Table 4 could partly reflect data augmentation rather than curriculum learning benefits; distribution and contribution of interaction patterns not clearly characterized

Limited scope of evaluation: All benchmarks focus on speech-to-text/speech-to-speech understanding; no evaluation on dialogue quality, multi-turn conversations, real-world metrics, or non-English speech
Data selection methodology introduces potential bias: selecting 26K hours based on WER of synthesized speech could bias results toward specific acoustic characteristics

strengths: Well-motivated technical problem addressing frequency mismatch between speech and text tokens with clear practical importance
Achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks (OpenAudioBench 69.24, Big Bench Audio 66.3) with >10 point margins, plus competitive performance on VoiceBench and UltraEval-Audio
Significant computational efficiency gains (50% GPU hours reduction) while maintaining competitive speech quality (UTMOS 4.29)
Elegant dual-resolution design combining grouped input (5Hz) for efficiency with ungrouped generation via Speech Refined Head
Comprehensive ablation studies (Table 4) clearly demonstrating the contribution of each component (CSE, SRH, SRH-pretraining, CoM-Mixing)
Thorough experimental validation including data scaling analysis, grouping factor analysis, and multiple evaluation metrics (UTMOS, ASR-WER, accuracy)
Strong reproducibility with detailed implementation details, training specifications, and use of released model components
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily combines existing techniques (token grouping from Chen et al. 2024a, Chain-of-Modality from Zhang et al. 2023a, Core-Cocktail inspired by Xiao et al. 2024) rather than introducing fundamental innovations
Significant speech-text alignment gap with ASR-WER of 11.2 vs. Qwen2.5-Omni's 3.48 (~3x worse), limiting practical utility for voice conversation applications despite acknowledgment
Heavy reliance on synthesized training data (~26K hours) with insufficient analysis of real vs. synthetic speech performance; raises generalization concerns for real-world deployment
Lack of principled justification for design choices—grouping factor k=5 appears empirically optimal but lacks theoretical grounding; Core-Cocktail training seems ad-hoc with limited generalizability
Restricted scope with evaluation exclusively on English benchmarks, no multilingual analysis, and limited to ~7B parameter class; unclear scaling properties to other model sizes

Speech quality metrics on relatively new benchmarks (OpenAudioBench, Big Bench Audio); SOTA claim would be stronger with improvements on more established VoiceBench benchmark (currently competitive, not SOTA)
Missing analysis of design mechanisms—why does grouping improve both understanding and generation? Counterintuitive result deserves deeper investigation
No qualitative analysis, failure case examination, or detailed error comparison with baselines; no discussion of when/why the model succeeds or fails
Training complexity with Core-Cocktail requiring careful two-stage tuning (α=0, specific learning rates); generalizability to other base models unclear
